newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ PM says would back "right" compulsory super.
newsitem.headline: NZ PM says would back "right" compulsory super.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Wednesday said he would support a compulsory superannuation scheme in this September's referendum if the right scheme was proposed.
"I would be happy to support a compulsory scheme if it was the right one," Bolger told Reuters.
But he would not be drawn on the nature of the scheme he favoured.
He said he would not actively promote a scheme, but would make his views known.
The National-New Zealand First coalition government agreed to hold a referendum on compulsory superannuation during their coalition talks.
On Tuesday, Justice Minister Doug Graham said a postal ballot on compulsory superannuation would be held over a three week period in September.

The scheme to make everyone contribute a portion of income to an individual pension savings scheme -- initially three percent in 1998/99, rising to eight percent by 2002 -- was championed by New Zealand First and opposed by National during last year's election campaign.
Graham said the government would consider itself bound by the result if it was approved by a simple majority of those voting, irrespective of voter turnout.
The final result will be declared in early October.

A core group of officials, including a private sector person, has been established to design the scheme, drawing on the superannuation policy announced by New Zealand First, and the principles outlined by the Todd Taskforce on private provision for retirement.
The group will consult with other government agencies and with industry as detail of the scheme is developed.
"The coalition government, as a government, will remain neutral on the proposal and each MP is entitled to argue for or against the scheme," Graham said.
